catalog_locator: p. 983 (accent paragraph, below the diphthong table; extract, full-volume scan p. 1057) and p. 986 (extract; verb-accent remarks).
catalog_quote: L’accent est en général sur la pénultième syllabe, quand le mot en contient deux ou trois; sur l’antépénultième, quand le mot a plus de trois syllabes. Cependant α) les mots composés gardent souvent les deux accents des composants, tout en forçant un peu plus celui du mot principal. Ex. akufálu, dáilabílabi. β) Les mots se terminant par une diphtongue descendante, autre que l’-ai du suffixe circonstanciel, y reportent leur accent, ex. kabói̯, udái̯, mais banúai̯. γ) Les suffixes de relation intransitive na, ka, mu̯i, -tsi (v. ci-dessous) transportent l’accent à la pénultième syllabe. Ex. adavána, adaváka, adavámu̯i, adavátsi, mais adávau, adávamu et adavamái̯. [p. 986] ... à la 3e pers. sing. ce suffixe est souvent omis, quand le verbe n’a pas d’autre suffixe, et n’est pas au passé. Ex. oyame boloma fe alá le chien mordra le porc. Remarquez cependant l’accent sur la dernière syllabe. ... La forme passive est inconnue en kuni. En revanche, la forme neutre est souvent employée. Elle se distingue de l’active, par l’absence du suffixe de relation transitive, et souvent par le changement d’accent. Ex. a úka je me mets dans, a uká je mets dans.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kuni (kuni1263, Oceanic, Central Province PNG) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Francard et al. 2001 'L'accent belge: Mythes et réalités', is a Glottolog machine mis-assignment (the saved BibTeX record says language code 'Kuni [kse] (computerized assignment from \"mythes\")'); it is a chapter on the Belgian French regional accent and irrelevant, priority none. The best first-hand stress statement is Egidi 1913 (Anthropos 8, p. 983; already held by the project at from an earlier reading, re-read and verified against the page scan): accent generally penultimate in 2-3-syllable words and antepenultimate in longer words, with compound, final-falling-diphthong and suffix-conditioned exceptions, plus accent alternations marking verb forms (pp. 986-987). Pawley 1975 (held by the project) is silent on stress. Jones 2020 (Oceanic Linguistics 59, doi:10.1353/ol.2020.0004) remains unread behind Project MUSE; low priority for stress. direct download and Crossref/Glottolog records were used instead.

new_statements.quote: L'accent est en général sur la pénultième syllabe, quand le mot en contient deux ou trois; sur l'antépénultième, quand le mot a plus de trois syllabes. Cependant α) les mots composés gardent souvent les deux accents des composants, tout en forçant un peu plus celui du mot principal. Ex. akufálu, dáilabílabi. β) Les mots se terminant par une diphtongue descendante, autre que l'-ai du suffixe circonstanciel, y reportent leur accent, ex. kabói̯, udái̯, mais banúai̯. γ) Les suffixes de relation intransitive na, ka, mu̯i, -tsi (v. ci-dessous) transportent l'accent à la pénultième syllabe. Ex. adavána, adaváka, adavámu̯i, adavátsi, mais adávau, adávamu et adavamái̯.
new_statements.translation: The accent is in general on the penultimate syllable when the word contains two or three syllables; on the antepenultimate when the word has more than three syllables. However (a) compound words often keep both accents of their components, while making that of the principal word somewhat stronger, e.g. akufálu, dáilabílabi; (b) words ending in a falling diphthong, other than the -ai of the circumstantial suffix, carry their accent on it, e.g. kabói, udái, but banúai; (c) the intransitive-relation suffixes na, ka, mui, -tsi shift the accent to the penultimate syllable, e.g. adavána, adaváka, adavámui, adavátsi, but adávau, adávamu and adavamái.
new_statements.citation: Egidi, Vincenzo M. 1913. Mythes et légendes des Kuni, British New-Guinea. Anthropos 8: 978-1009.
new_statements.locator: p. 983, section 'II. La langue kuni' (PDF page 6 of the extract = page 1057 of the full-volume scan); further remarks p. 986
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, extract page 6 = Anthropos 8 p. 983 (running head 'Mythes et Légendes des Kuni, British New-Guinea. 983'), verified against the 200-dpi render : the paragraph 'L'accent est en général sur la pénultième syllabe, quand le mot en contient deux ou trois; sur l'antépénultième, quand le mot a plus de trois syllabes. Cependant α).. akufálu, dáilabílabi. β).. kabói̯, udái̯, mais banúai̯. γ).. adavána, adaváka, adavámu̯i, adavátsi, mais adávau, adávamu et adavamái̯.' is there word for word, diacritics included (the extracted text garbles the acutes, the image does not). The p. 986 remarks are also as reported (extract page 9): 'à la 3e pers. sing. ce suffixe est souvent omis.. Ex. oyam…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is penultimate in di- and trisyllables and antepenultimate in words of four or more syllables; a word-final falling diphthong attracts the accent (except the circumstantial suffix -ai); certain verbal suffixes (na, ka, mui, tsi) pull the accent onto the penult while others (-au, -mu, -mai) do not; compounds retain the accent of each member with the head's stronger. On p. 986 Egidi adds that a 3sg transitive verb with the suffix dropped keeps accent on the final syllable, and that 'neutral' (intransitive) vs active forms are often distinguished by an accent shift (a uíka 'I put myself in' vs a uiká 'I put in'), i.e. accent has some morphological load.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only for compounds: both members keep their accent, the principal word's being somewhat stronger (akufálu, dáilabílabi).
new_statements.exceptions: Final falling diphthongs take the accent (kabói̯, udái̯) except circumstantial -ai (banúai̯); suffixes na/ka/mu̯i/tsi shift accent to penult, -au/-mu/-mai̯ do not (adávau, adávamu, adavamái̯); 3sg verb with omitted transitive suffix is final-accented; active vs neutral verb pairs differ by accent (a uíka / a uiká).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in the Dilava variety as transcribed by a resident missionary (1904-1907); 'en général' hedges the rule; the antepenult clause for 4+-syllable words makes this a length-conditioned penult/antepenult system rather than pure fixed penult, and the verb remarks show some morphological conditioning. Accent is marked with acute on cited forms throughout the sketch and texts.
new_statements.identity_note: Egidi describes the Kuni spoken at Dilava (his Sacred Heart mission station on the upper St Joseph/Aroa, 1904-1907), explicitly 'la langue parlée à Dilava', and notes dialect differences elsewhere (Devadeva replaces k by aspiration; right-bank groups Idoido, Maimai, Yaifa shift several consonants; Inauveida tinged with Pokau). This is the same language as Glottolog kuni1263 / ISO kse (modern centre Bakoiudu). Caution: Glottolog's kse bibliography also lists R. Fumey's SIL literacy booklets, which belong to Kuni-Boazi [kvg] of Western Province, a different (non-Austronesian) language.

new_statements.quote: The present-imperfect is further distinct in having marked word stress on the subject marking syllable, though the rule is not always observed with polysyllabic verb words. However, this means that even when there is no morphologically marked distinction between past and present, speakers can still signal present-imperfect tense-aspect phonologically, i.e. in speech. [fn. 9, p. 434:] In fact this verb would be pronounced è-mai with stress on the subject-marking prefix.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Egidi 1913 (the catalog's existing statement: penultimate in 2-3 syllable words, antepenultimate in longer words, with morphological re-anchoring). Jones adds one morphological exception: present-imperfect verbs carry stress on the subject-marking prefix (word-initial in the verb word), a tense-marking use of accent parallel to Egidi's remark (pp. 986-987) that accent alternation marks verb forms (a úka vs a uká). It neither confirms nor contradicts the default penultimate/antepenultimate placement, which it does not discuss. Jones also names two unpublished Kuni sources not in our list: Eschlimann, Henri 1935 'Grammaire Kuni' (Pacific Manuscripts Bureau, AU PMB MS 661) and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress rule is stated. The only statement is grammatical: in the present-imperfect verb form, word stress falls on the subject-marking prefix syllable (the first syllable of the verb word, e.g. è-mai 's/he comes'), which distinguishes it from the past (i-mai) even where the prefixes are otherwise identical; the rule 'is not always observed with polysyllabic verb words'. Nothing on nouns, secondary stress, or default placement; the Table 1 form 'fakàma-' (subjunctive 1st incl.) carries a grave accent that is not explained.
new_statements.exceptions: The prefix-stress rule of the present-imperfect 'is not always observed with polysyllabic verb words'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the same language as the catalog: Jones 2019 works from Egidi's 1906 Kuni texts, Eschlimann's 1935 manuscript grammar and his own fieldnotes, and places Kuni in the Nuclear West Central Papuan linkage alongside Mekeo, Roro/Waima and Motu (p. 433); Ross 1988 lists its Kuni sources as Egidi 1907, 1913a, 1913b and an informant Barnabas Maua of Bakoiudu (pp. 398, 406) and treats Kuni in the Central Papuan subgroup of Papuan Tip. No dialect is singled out.

sources.note: Only openly accessible modern linguist's note on Kuni grammar (fieldwork c. 1981 plus Egidi and Eschlimann). Silent on the general word-stress rule but states that the present-imperfect is marked by word stress on the subject-marking prefix (è-mai 'is coming' vs i-mai 'came'), 'not always observed with polysyllabic verb words' -- a grammatical stress alternation to record alongside Egidi's penult default.
